title: Inclusive = In fact/Actually (correcting)
definition: Use 'in fact' or 'actually' when someone is wrong and you clarify the truth.
example2: “Achei que você não gostava de festa.” – “Adoro. Inclusive, vou em todas.” -> “Actually, I go to all of them.”

title: Inclusive = In fact/Actually (insisting)
definition: Use when you insist something is true even if doubted.
example2: “Ninguém me avisou.” – “Eu avisei sim. Inclusive, eu te mandei mensagem ontem.” -> “In fact, I sent you a message yesterday.”
image_url: Use 'in fact' to emphasize you are telling the truth.

title: Inclusive = What's more (stronger point)
definition: Add a second point that is even more important or extreme.
example2: “O trânsito estava horrível. Inclusive, fiquei duas horas parado.” -> “What's more, I was stuck for two hours.”
image_url: 'What's more' is conversational and common in spoken English.

title: Inclusive = On top of that (negative addition)
definition: Use to add another bad thing to a list of problems.
example2: “Ele é muito enrolado. Inclusive, perdeu o voo semana passada.” -> “On top of that, he missed his flight last week.”
image_url: 'On top of that' is very natural in conversation.

title: Inclusive = Even (surprising person)
definition: Use before a surprising person or thing that is unexpected in the context.
example2: “Todo mundo reclamou, inclusive o Paulo que nunca fala nada.” -> “Everyone complained, even Paulo, who never says anything.”
image_url: Place 'even' directly before the surprising word.

title: Inclusive = Even (surprising situation)
definition: Use for unexpected actions or conditions.
example2: “Ele se dá bem com todos, inclusive com o chefe chato.” -> “He gets along with everyone, even with the annoying boss.”
image_url: 'Even' can go before a noun phrase or prepositional phrase.

title: Inclusive = Including (neutral list)
definition: Simple enumeration, no surprise or emphasis.
example2: “Precisamos de várias coisas, inclusive leite e pão.” -> “We need several things, including milk and bread.”
image_url: Never use 'even' for neutral lists – it would sound strange.

title: Inclusive = Including (question form)
definition: When asking if something is part of a group.
example2: “A promoção vale para todos os produtos? Inclusive os da prateleira de cima?” -> “Including the ones on the top shelf?”

title: Common mistake #1 (false friend)
definition: Never start an English sentence with 'Inclusive'
example2: ❌ 'Inclusive, I like pizza.' ✅ 'Actually, I like pizza.'
example3: ❌ 'Inclusive, she arrived late.' ✅ 'In fact, she arrived late.'
description: Delete 'Inclusive' and replace with 'Actually' or 'In fact'.

title: Common mistake #2 (including vs even)
example2: ❌ 'She speaks three languages, inclusive French.' ✅ 'She speaks three languages, including French.' (list)

title: Common mistake #3 (just stating fact)
definition: Don't use 'including' to state a fact
example2: ❌ 'Inclusive, it's raining.' ✅ 'In fact, it's raining.'
description: Use 'in fact' or 'actually' for simple facts.

title: Tip for A2 learners
example2: When you hear 'inclusive', ask: Correcting? → actually. Surprising? → even. Listing? → including.
example3: Practice with YouTube or TV series – count how many times you hear 'inclusive'.
description: The tone of voice gives you the clue.
